requirement: Management should set out the organisation's overall direction for information security in an approved, top-level policy, supported by topic-specific policies. These should be communicated to staff and relevant third parties, acknowledged, and reviewed at planned intervals or when significant changes occur.
current_state: A six-page 'IT Security Policy' was drafted by the CTO in 2024 to answer a partner bank's due-diligence questionnaire. It has not been approved by the CEO or the Board, carries no version control, owner or review date, and sits in the CTO's personal Google Drive. Employees are not asked to read or acknowledge it. No topic-specific policies exist (access control, acceptable use, cryptography, supplier security, incident management, data retention); some rules are described informally on the engineering wiki.
evidence_requested: Approved Information Security Policy with version history and management sign-off; index of topic-specific policies; policy communication and acknowledgement records (HRMS export); policy review schedule and minutes of the last review.
gap: A policy exists in draft only. There is no management approval, no communication or acknowledgement by staff, no review cycle and no topic-specific policies, so staff have no authoritative rules and SecurePay cannot demonstrate management direction to RBI, partner banks or a certification auditor.
recommendation: Refresh the draft into a concise Information Security Policy aligned to ISO/IEC 27001 and PCI DSS and have it approved by the CEO. Build a policy framework of about eight topic-specific policies (access control, acceptable use, cryptography and key management, supplier security, incident management, logging and monitoring, secure development, data protection and retention). Publish through the HRMS with annual e-acknowledgement and set an annual review date.

requirement: The organisation should collect information about threats that are relevant to it, analyse that information to produce useful intelligence (strategic, tactical and operational), and use it to inform risk decisions and to adjust its security controls.
current_state: There is no defined threat intelligence process or owner. Engineers occasionally notice security news on social media or in community Slack groups. Nobody is responsible for monitoring CERT-In advisories, AWS security bulletins or disclosures affecting the technology stack (Node.js, PostgreSQL, React, npm packages). A 2025 CERT-In advisory on phishing campaigns targeting payment companies was not reviewed or acted upon. No threat profile exists for SecurePay as an online payment aggregator.
evidence_requested: Threat intelligence procedure and named owner; list of subscribed sources; log of advisories received, triaged and actioned; periodic threat landscape briefing to management; evidence of intelligence feeding into controls (e.g. WAF rule or detection updates).
gap: Threat information is not collected, analysed or used. SecurePay relies on chance awareness, so threats that specifically target payment platforms (card-testing and enumeration attacks, credential stuffing against merchant logins, malicious npm packages, BEC targeting settlement teams) are not anticipated in its controls.
recommendation: Assign threat intelligence ownership to the Information Security Manager. Subscribe to CERT-In advisories, AWS security bulletins, GitHub security advisories and vendor feeds, and join a payments or fintech information-sharing community. Hold a fortnightly 30-minute triage with a simple log of advisories and actions taken. Produce a one-page quarterly threat briefing for leadership. Once monitoring is in place, feed indicators of compromise into AWS WAF and GuardDuty threat lists.

control_name: Inventory of information and other associated assets
requirement: The organisation should identify its information and the assets associated with it (hardware, software, cloud services, data stores, people-held knowledge), record them in an inventory that is kept up to date, and assign each an owner responsible for its protection.
current_state: About 80% of AWS resources carry 'env' and 'service' tags, and HR and Admin keep a laptop register in a spreadsheet (serial number and assigned user). However, there is no inventory of information assets (merchant KYC files, transaction data, settlement files, customer support records). SaaS applications are not catalogued; an informal count during the assessment found about 25. Owners and classification are not assigned, and the laptop register was last updated four months ago.
evidence_requested: Asset register(s) showing owner, classification and location; AWS Config or resource inventory export; SaaS discovery report (e.g. from Google Workspace OAuth app list); reconciliation of the laptop register to the MDM; records of periodic asset reviews.
gap: The inventory covers only part of the cloud infrastructure and endpoints. It omits information assets and SaaS, lacks owners and classification, and is not kept current. This weakens risk assessment, access reviews and the data mapping SecurePay needs for the DPDP Act.
recommendation: Create a single asset register (spreadsheet or lightweight GRC tool) that covers information assets, applications and SaaS, cloud services and endpoints. Give every entry an owner and a classification (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). Enforce mandatory AWS tags through AWS Organizations tag policies, reconcile the register monthly against AWS Config and the MDM, and have owners review it quarterly.
owner: Information Security Manager with asset owners

requirement: The organisation should define and apply processes to manage the security risks that come from using suppliers' products and services. This includes assessing suppliers before engaging them and agreeing how they may access and handle the organisation's information.
current_state: Customer support is outsourced to a Pune-based BPO ('SupportCo', 12 agents). Agents work in a SaaS helpdesk and a read-only internal support console that shows customer names, phone numbers, email addresses, masked card numbers (last four digits), UPI IDs and transaction history. The vendor was selected on cost and no security due diligence was done. The master services agreement has a generic confidentiality clause but no security requirements, breach notification, audit rights or data return and deletion obligations. Agents share three logins to the support console. There is no supplier inventory or risk tiering for the roughly 25 SaaS and service providers in use.
evidence_requested: Supplier security policy; supplier inventory with risk tiering; due-diligence questionnaires and assurance reports (ISO 27001 certificate, SOC 2 report) for critical suppliers; contracts and data processing agreements with security schedules; list of supplier user accounts and access review records.
gap: There is no supplier security risk management. The highest-risk supplier has broad access to customer personal data through shared credentials and has no contractual security obligations. Under the DPDP Act, SupportCo is a Data Processor and SecurePay, as Data Fiduciary, remains accountable for any breach it causes.
recommendation: Publish a supplier security policy and build a supplier inventory with risk tiers (critical, high, medium, low). Assess SupportCo immediately using a security questionnaire and a site or virtual visit. Sign a data processing agreement with a security schedule covering minimum controls, incident notification within 6 hours (to support CERT-In timelines), audit rights, data return and deletion, and approval of sub-processors. Replace shared logins with named accounts protected by MFA, mask contact details agents do not need, and review supplier access quarterly.
owner: Head of Customer Operations; Head of Legal & Compliance

control_name: Information security for use of cloud services
requirement: The organisation should set up processes for acquiring, using, managing and exiting cloud services that match its security requirements, including a clear split of security responsibilities between the cloud provider and the organisation.
current_state: Production runs in AWS ap-south-1 (Mumbai) to meet RBI payment data localisation, using managed services (ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ, S3, KMS). Good practices are in place: S3 Block Public Access at account level, default encryption at rest, and AWS Organizations with separate production and non-production accounts. However, there is no cloud security policy or documented shared-responsibility matrix, AWS Security Hub and CIS benchmark checks are not enabled, teams adopt SaaS tools without security review, and there is no exit or portability plan.
evidence_requested: Cloud security policy or standard; shared-responsibility matrix per service; evidence of reviewing AWS assurance reports (PCI DSS AOC, SOC 2) via AWS Artifact; cloud security posture findings (Security Hub); SaaS approval records; cloud exit strategy.
gap: The technical foundations are sound, but cloud use is not governed. There is no policy, no responsibility matrix, no continuous posture assessment, uncontrolled SaaS adoption and no exit strategy.
recommendation: Approve a cloud security standard and document the shared-responsibility split for each AWS service and critical SaaS application. Enable AWS Security Hub with the CIS AWS Foundations and PCI DSS standards across all accounts. Download and review AWS's PCI DSS AOC and SOC 2 report every year. Introduce a lightweight SaaS approval workflow with a security and privacy checklist, and document a cloud exit and portability plan that can be shown to regulators.

control_name: Information security incident management planning and preparation
requirement: The organisation should prepare to handle security incidents by defining, documenting and communicating its incident management processes, roles and responsibilities, so that incidents are dealt with quickly, effectively and consistently.
current_state: No incident response plan exists. Incidents are handled ad hoc in a Slack channel by whichever engineer notices. In March 2026 a credential-stuffing attack on merchant dashboard logins was handled over two days without severity classification, a root-cause record, or a decision on whether CERT-In (6-hour) reporting or notification to the acquiring bank was required. Staff do not know how or to whom to report a suspected incident, and there is no contact list for CERT-In, RBI, the acquiring bank or legal counsel.
evidence_requested: Incident response plan and procedures; incident response team roles (RACI); severity matrix; regulatory notification matrix (CERT-In, RBI, Data Protection Board, card networks via the acquirer); incident log; tabletop exercise reports; on-call rota.
gap: There is no defined incident management capability. Regulatory deadlines (CERT-In reporting within 6 hours, DPDP breach intimation to the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals, RBI reporting) cannot be met reliably, and lessons from incidents are not captured.
recommendation: Approve an incident response plan covering preparation, detection, triage and severity, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident review. Name an incident response team with deputies and a 24x7 on-call rota. Build a regulatory notification matrix with ready-to-use templates. Set up one reporting channel (security@ mailbox plus a Slack workflow). Run a tabletop exercise (card-testing attack and ransomware scenarios) within 90 days and every year after that, and consider an incident response retainer.

requirement: The organisation should identify and meet the requirements for preserving privacy and protecting personal data that apply to it under law, regulation and contract.
current_state: A privacy policy is published on the website and the checkout flow records consent. Card data is never stored (it is tokenised by the partner processor) and Aadhaar numbers are masked during merchant KYC. However, there is no inventory of what personal data is processed and where, and no retention and deletion schedule (KYC documents of off-boarded merchants are kept indefinitely in S3). No DPDP Act gap analysis has been done, there is no process for Data Principal requests (access, correction, erasure, grievance), and nobody is formally accountable for data protection. Production data is periodically copied to the staging environment for debugging.
evidence_requested: Personal data inventory and records of processing; DPDP Act gap assessment; privacy notices and consent records; retention schedule and deletion logs; Data Principal request and grievance log; appointment of a privacy owner and grievance contact; breach notification procedure; data processing agreements with processors.
gap: Some basic privacy measures exist, but SecurePay cannot demonstrate DPDP Act compliance. There is no data mapping, no retention limits, no rights handling, no breach notification procedure and no accountable owner, and production personal data is used in non-production environments.
recommendation: Carry out a DPDP Act gap assessment and build a personal data inventory with data flow maps. Define a retention schedule that respects statutory record-keeping minimums (RBI, PMLA) and automate it with S3 lifecycle rules. Implement a Data Principal request and grievance process with SLAs. Make the Head of Legal & Compliance the accountable privacy owner. Prohibit production personal data in non-production environments (use masked or synthetic data) and add DPDP breach notification to the incident response plan.

requirement: Background verification checks should be carried out on candidates before they join and, where appropriate, on an ongoing basis. Checks should follow applicable laws and be proportionate to the business need, the sensitivity of the information the person will access and the risks involved.
current_state: All employees go through pre-joining background verification by an accredited third-party agency (identity, address, education, previous employment and criminal records database check). Reports are retained in the HR system. Roles with privileged or financial access also get an additional reference check. System access is granted only after verification clears, as recorded in the HR onboarding checklist.
evidence_requested: Screening procedure or HR onboarding checklist; sample of background verification reports for recent joiners (e.g. 10 of the last 15 hires); candidate consent forms; evidence that checks were completed before system access was granted.
gap: No significant gap. Observation: screening requirements by role are not written down in a formal procedure, and equivalent screening of vendor staff (SupportCo agents) is not required contractually (addressed under A.5.19).
recommendation: Document a role-based screening standard. Require suppliers whose staff access SecurePay data to confirm equivalent screening. Consider periodic re-screening for privileged and finance roles.

control_name: Information security awareness, education and training
requirement: Staff and relevant interested parties should receive security awareness, education and training suited to their role, along with regular updates on the organisation's security policies and procedures.
current_state: New joiners receive a 20-minute induction slide on password hygiene and phishing. There is no annual refresher, no role-based training for developers (secure coding), finance (payment fraud and business email compromise) or operations (social engineering), and no phishing simulation. Completion is not tracked, and SupportCo agents receive no SecurePay-specific security training.
evidence_requested: Training plan and content; LMS completion records; phishing simulation results; role-based training records for developers and finance; evidence of training for third-party staff.
gap: Awareness is limited to a one-off induction with no refresher, no role-based content, no measurement and no coverage of vendor staff. People remain a weak link against phishing and BEC, which are among the most common initial attack vectors in financial services.
recommendation: Launch an annual awareness programme (30-45 minute modules) with tracked completion and a target of at least 95%. Run quarterly phishing simulations and track report rates. Add role-based training: OWASP Top 10 and secure coding for engineers, payment fraud and BEC for finance and operations, and personal data handling for support. Require SupportCo agents to complete the same module, and report metrics to management every quarter.
owner: Information Security Manager; HR & Admin Manager

requirement: When people work remotely, security measures should be in place to protect information that is accessed, processed or stored outside the organisation's premises.
current_state: SecurePay works in a hybrid model (three office days a week). All staff use company-issued laptops enrolled in the MDM with enforced full-disk encryption (FileVault or BitLocker), a five-minute screen lock, automatic OS updates and endpoint anti-malware. Corporate applications are reached through Google Workspace SSO with enforced MFA. Remote working rules (public Wi-Fi, screen privacy, no company data on personal devices) are in the employee handbook and acknowledged at joining.
evidence_requested: Remote working policy (handbook section) with acknowledgement records; MDM compliance report showing encryption and screen-lock status; sample device configurations; SSO and MFA enforcement settings.
gap: No significant gap. Observation: the MDM report showed 3 of 54 laptops with OS updates pending for more than 30 days, and personal mobile phones can access Gmail and Slack without any device management.
recommendation: Make device compliance (supported OS version, encryption) a condition of SSO access. Apply basic management or app protection policies to mobile devices that access Workspace and Slack. Reconcile the MDM device list with the asset register every month.

requirement: Secure areas should be protected by appropriate entry controls and access points so that only authorised people can get in.
current_state: SecurePay occupies one floor of a managed office building in Bengaluru. Building security controls entry with a reception desk, visitor registration against photo ID, and RFID access cards. The SecurePay floor has card-controlled doors whose logs the facility provider keeps for 90 days. Apart from a Wi-Fi access point and ISP router in a locked comms cabinet, no servers or network equipment are on site. Access cards are deactivated as part of the leaver checklist.
evidence_requested: Facility access procedure; access card issuance and revocation records reconciled to the HR leavers list; visitor logs; sample of the facility provider's door access logs; CCTV coverage of entry points.
gap: No significant gap. Observation: visitors are not escorted on the SecurePay floor once they have registered at reception, and active access cards are not reviewed periodically.
recommendation: Introduce visible visitor badges and an escort rule on the SecurePay floor. Reconcile active access cards with the HR roster every quarter.

control_name: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
requirement: Before equipment containing storage media is disposed of or re-used, the organisation should check that any sensitive data and licensed software have been removed or securely overwritten.
current_state: Laptops returned by leavers are reissued to new joiners after the previous user's profile is deleted manually; there is no secure wipe or OS reinstallation. Six old laptops were sold to an informal buyer in 2025 with no data sanitisation and no certificate. There is no disposal procedure or disposal log. Disks are encrypted, but recovery keys are not rotated when a laptop is reassigned.
evidence_requested: Equipment disposal and re-use procedure; disposal log recording the sanitisation method; certificates of data destruction from an authorised e-waste recycler; MDM wipe records.
gap: There is no controlled process for re-use or disposal. Residual data (source code, credentials, customer data exports) could be recovered by the next user or by a third-party buyer, and selling to informal buyers may also breach the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.
recommendation: Adopt a procedure that requires an MDM-initiated wipe or factory reset (cryptographic erase) before any laptop is reissued. Dispose of equipment only through an authorised e-waste recycler that provides certificates of data destruction, and keep a disposal log linked to the asset register.

requirement: The allocation and use of privileged access rights should be restricted and managed so that only authorised people hold them, only for as long as needed, and their use is controlled and monitored.
current_state: Five engineers, two of whom have since moved to non-infrastructure roles, permanently hold the AWS 'AdministratorAccess' policy through IAM users. The production account's root user is used occasionally for billing tasks; its credentials sit in a password manager vault shared by three people. Production PostgreSQL is accessed with a shared 'postgres' superuser credential known to seven engineers. No privileged access review has ever been carried out, and privileged activity is not monitored.
evidence_requested: Privileged access management procedure; list of privileged accounts across AWS, databases, GitHub organisation owners and Google Workspace super admins; approval records; privileged access review records; root account usage logs (CloudTrail); break-glass procedure.
gap: Privileged access to the production cloud and database is excessive, permanent and shared, with no approval, review or monitoring. A single compromised engineer laptop or credential would give an attacker full control of the payment platform and customer data.
recommendation: Move to AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) with MFA, role-based permission sets and time-bound (just-in-time) elevation for administrative roles, and remove IAM users with admin rights. Lock away the root user (hardware MFA kept in a safe, alerting on any root login, documented break-glass procedure). Replace the shared database superuser with individual IAM-authenticated roles and session logging. Review privileged access monthly for six months, then quarterly, and limit GitHub organisation owners and Workspace super admins to two people each.

requirement: Secure authentication technologies and procedures should be in place, matched to how sensitive the information is and how access is restricted, for example multi-factor authentication for higher-risk access.
current_state: Google Workspace SSO with enforced 2-step verification covers email and most internal SaaS, and AWS IAM users have MFA. However, the internal 'Ops Console' (used by operations and support to view merchant and customer data and to initiate refunds) uses username and password only, with no account lockout. SupportCo agents use shared credentials without MFA. The merchant dashboard offers optional OTP 2FA, used by about 18% of merchants; this was the target of the March 2026 credential-stuffing attack. The merchant password policy requires only 8 characters and does not check for breached passwords.
evidence_requested: Authentication standard; SSO and MFA enforcement reports (Workspace, AWS); authentication configuration of the Ops Console and merchant dashboard (MFA, lockout, rate limiting); results of login rate-limit testing; list of accounts without MFA.
gap: Corporate identities are well protected, but the internal and customer-facing applications that expose personal data and can move money (refunds) lack MFA, account lockout and brute-force protection.
recommendation: Put the Ops Console behind Google Workspace SSO with enforced MFA and give vendor agents named accounts. Make 2FA mandatory for merchant users with refund or payout permissions and strongly encourage it for everyone else. Add rate limiting, progressive lockout and bot protection (AWS WAF rate-based rules, CAPTCHA) to login endpoints, and check new passwords against breached-password lists. Consider phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 security keys) for administrators.

requirement: The organisation should get timely information about technical vulnerabilities in the systems it uses, assess how exposed it is, and take suitable action (patching or other mitigation) within defined timeframes.
current_state: GitHub Dependabot alerts are enabled on all repositories and container base images are rebuilt monthly. An annual VAPT is performed by a CERT-In empanelled auditor (last in January 2026) because partner banks require it. However, 4 of the 11 High findings from that VAPT are still open nine months later, including an insecure direct object reference (IDOR) in the merchant reports API and missing rate limiting on the OTP verification endpoint. There are 142 open Dependabot alerts (17 Critical or High). No remediation SLAs exist, containers and cloud workloads are not scanned, vulnerability metrics are not tracked, and the quarterly external ASV scans required by PCI DSS have not started.
evidence_requested: Vulnerability management procedure with SLAs; VAPT reports and remediation tracker; Dependabot and SCA dashboards; container image scan results (Amazon ECR or Inspector); ASV scan reports; risk acceptance records for exceptions.
gap: Vulnerabilities are found but not fixed in a timely or tracked way. There are no SLAs, owners or exception process, and container, cloud and ASV scanning are missing.
recommendation: Define remediation SLAs by severity (e.g. Critical 7 days, High 30 days, Medium 90 days) with documented risk acceptance for exceptions. Close the four open High VAPT findings within 30 days and get them retested. Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector) and run it in CI. Work through the Dependabot backlog in a weekly triage. Start quarterly ASV scans, move to twice-yearly VAPT plus retests after major releases, and report vulnerability ageing to management every month.

requirement: Security configurations, including baselines, for hardware, software, services and networks should be defined, documented, implemented, monitored and reviewed.
current_state: About 70% of AWS infrastructure is defined in Terraform and changes are peer-reviewed through pull requests. The rest (a legacy EC2 bastion host, some security groups and the AWS WAF rules) was created by hand in the console. No hardening baselines are documented (e.g. CIS Benchmarks for AWS, PostgreSQL or container images), there is no drift detection, and AWS Config is enabled only in the production account with no rules.
evidence_requested: Configuration management standard and hardening baselines; Terraform repository and pull request history; AWS Config rules or conformance pack results; drift detection reports; configuration exception register.
gap: Infrastructure-as-code adoption is good but incomplete. Without defined secure baselines, drift detection or compliance monitoring, misconfigurations, a leading cause of cloud breaches, may go unnoticed.
recommendation: Adopt CIS AWS Foundations and the relevant CIS Docker and PostgreSQL benchmarks as baselines. Import the remaining hand-built resources into Terraform and add policy-as-code checks (e.g. Checkov or tfsec) to the CI pipeline. Enable AWS Config conformance packs in all accounts with alerts on drift. Retire the legacy bastion host in favour of AWS Systems Manager Session Manager.

requirement: Backup copies of information, software and systems should be kept and tested regularly in line with an agreed backup policy.
current_state: Amazon RDS automated backups are enabled with 35-day retention and point-in-time recovery. Daily snapshots are copied to ap-south-2 (Hyderabad) and encrypted with a separate KMS key. S3 buckets holding KYC documents and settlement files have versioning and cross-region replication, and infrastructure can be rebuilt from Terraform. A documented backup standard sets RPO at 15 minutes and RTO at 4 hours. A restore of the production database into an isolated account was tested and documented in June 2026 (completed in 2 hours 40 minutes).
evidence_requested: Backup policy with RPO and RTO; AWS Backup or RDS configuration evidence; cross-region copy evidence; restore test reports; backup failure alerts.
gap: No significant gap. Observations: restore tests are not scheduled on a recurring basis; GitHub and Google Workspace data rely solely on the providers' own resilience; backups are not immutable (AWS Backup Vault Lock is not enabled), so a compromised administrator or ransomware could delete them.
recommendation: Schedule quarterly restore tests. Enable AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for critical backups. Add third-party backup for GitHub and Google Workspace, and alert on failed backup jobs.

requirement: Networks, systems and applications should be monitored for unusual behaviour, and appropriate action should be taken to evaluate possible security incidents.
current_state: AWS CloudTrail (management events) is enabled across the organisation, and load balancer and application logs go to CloudWatch Logs with 30-day retention. CloudWatch alarms exist only for availability and performance (CPU, HTTP 5xx rates). Nobody reviews security logs. Amazon GuardDuty and VPC Flow Logs are disabled, and there is no SIEM or alerting on security events such as root logins, IAM policy changes, bulk data exports or unusual refund volumes. The March 2026 credential-stuffing attack was detected through a merchant complaint about 19 hours after it began. Related observation (A.8.15): 30-day log retention falls short of the 180 days required by the CERT-In Directions (April 2022) and the 12 months required by PCI DSS.
evidence_requested: Logging and monitoring standard; inventory of log sources and retention settings; SIEM or alert use-case catalogue; alert triage records; GuardDuty findings history; evidence of regular log review; escalation procedure.
gap: Logs are collected but not monitored. There is no capability to detect security events in a high-value payment environment, and log retention does not meet CERT-In or PCI DSS requirements.
recommendation: Enable GuardDuty, VPC Flow Logs, S3 data events for sensitive buckets and Security Hub now. Keep logs for at least one year (with 180 days readily available in India) in a dedicated, write-protected log archive account. Implement an initial set of 10-15 high-priority alerts (root or break-glass use, IAM changes, high-severity GuardDuty findings, WAF spikes, login failure spikes, abnormal refund or payout activity) routed to the on-call engineer. Within 6-12 months adopt a SIEM or engage a managed detection and response (MDR) provider for 24x7 coverage.

requirement: Rules for using cryptography effectively should be defined and applied, including how cryptographic keys are generated, stored, rotated, used and destroyed.
current_state: All external endpoints enforce TLS 1.2 or higher with strong cipher suites (SSL Labs grade A) and HSTS. Data at rest in RDS, S3 and EBS is encrypted with AWS KMS customer-managed keys that rotate automatically every year, and key policies limit use to service roles. Card data is never stored: the card number is captured in the partner processor's hosted fields and replaced by a token. Webhooks to merchants are signed with HMAC-SHA256, and partner bank API credentials are kept in AWS Secrets Manager.
evidence_requested: Cryptography and key management policy; TLS scan results; KMS key inventory, rotation settings and key policies; encryption-at-rest configuration; tokenisation architecture and the partner processor's PCI DSS AOC; review of the webhook signing implementation.
gap: No significant technical gap. Observation: these practices are not written down in a cryptography and key management policy, and certificates outside AWS Certificate Manager are not inventoried or monitored for expiry.
recommendation: Document a cryptography and key management policy (approved algorithms and key lengths, rotation, ownership, crypto-periods). Keep an inventory of certificates and keys with expiry alerts, and review crypto-agility (including post-quantum readiness) during the annual policy review.

requirement: Secure coding principles should be applied throughout software development so that code is written in a way that reduces the chance of security vulnerabilities.
current_state: GitHub branch protection requires one peer review before merging to main, and unit tests run in GitHub Actions. Developers use an ORM that prevents most SQL injection. However, there is no secure coding standard or checklist, reviews focus on functionality, and no SAST or secret-scanning tools are used. A scan of repository history during the assessment found nine hard-coded secrets, including a still-valid SMS gateway API key and a staging database password. Developers have had no secure coding training, and the IDOR found in the VAPT points to missing authorisation checks in the code.
evidence_requested: Secure coding standard (e.g. based on OWASP ASVS and Top 10); code review checklist; SAST, SCA and secret-scanning configuration and results; sample pull requests showing security review; developer training records; threat models for critical features.
gap: Secure coding depends on individual developers' knowledge. There is no standard, no automated security testing and no training, as shown by hard-coded secrets and authorisation flaws (IDOR) in the payment platform code.
recommendation: Rotate all exposed secrets immediately and move them to AWS Secrets Manager, then enable GitHub secret scanning with push protection. Adopt a secure coding standard based on OWASP ASVS Level 2 with a pull request security checklist (authorisation, input validation, logging, secrets). Add SAST (e.g. Semgrep or CodeQL) and SCA to CI, blocking merges on High findings. Run annual secure coding training, introduce lightweight threat modelling for new payment features, and nominate a security champion in each squad.
